match.reason: The bank point on the Roman Republic covers government, consuls, the Senate and the patrician-plebeian political divide, but it does not teach the social classes of patricians, plebeians and enslaved people or the legal power of the father over his household, so it is a related but different idea.

rejected.title: Roman society
card: Patricians
the old, wealthy families of Rome. In the early republic they held most of the power and the top jobs in government.
Plebeians
the ordinary free citizens, such as farmers, craftworkers and traders. Over time they won more rights, including officials who spoke up for them.
Enslaved people
people who were owned by others and had almost no rights. They did hard work on farms, in mines and in homes.
The father
the male head of a Roman family, called the paterfamilias. The law gave him power over everyone in his household, including his wife, children and slaves.
rejected.remember: Roman society had three main groups, and the father held legal power over his household.

a.q: In Roman society, who were the plebeians?
opts: Ordinary free citizens such as farmers and traders
Old, wealthy families who held the top jobs
People who were owned by others and had no rights
Fathers who held legal power over a household
a.why: Plebeians were the ordinary free citizens of Rome. Patricians were the old wealthy families, which is the most tempting wrong option, because both groups were free.
a.clue: Think of free people who were not from the old wealthy families.

b.q: Lucius is a Roman father in the early republic. His household includes his wife, his children and several enslaved workers. What does Roman law say about his place in the household?
opts: He had legal power over everyone in it
He had power over his slaves only
He shared legal power equally with his wife
He had power only if he was a patrician
b.why: Roman law gave the father legal power over his whole household, not just some of its members. The option about slaves only is tempting, but the card says his power covered his wife and children too.
b.clue: Look at how far the father's power reached.

version.title: Roman society
card: Patricians
a small group of old, wealthy families. A Roman was a patrician by birth into one of these families, and in the early republic they held most of the top jobs in government.
Plebeians
most free Roman citizens, from poor farmers to rich traders. Getting rich did not make a plebeian a patrician, but over time plebeians won the right to hold the top jobs too.
Enslaved people
people owned by others, many of them captured in war. The law treated them as property, and they worked on farms, in mines and in homes.
Paterfamilias
the father at the head of a Roman family. The law gave him power over his household, including his children and its enslaved people. Grown sons usually stayed under his power for as long as he lived.
version.remember: Patricians, plebeians and enslaved people had very different rights, and the paterfamilias held legal power over his household.

a.q: Gaius was born into an ordinary free Roman family. As an adult he grows very rich from trade. Which group does he belong to?
opts: Plebeians, as wealth did not change his group
Patricians, because his new wealth moves him up
Enslaved people, because he works for a living
No group, because traders sat outside all three
a.why: Patricians were patricians by birth into the old families, so Gaius stays a plebeian however rich he gets. The patrician option is tempting, but wealth alone did not change a Roman's group.
a.clue: Did money or birth decide a Roman's group?

b.q: Marcus is 30, married and runs his own farm. His father, Titus, is still alive. Under Roman law, who holds legal power over Marcus?
opts: Titus, as the head of the family while he lives
Marcus himself, as he is an adult with a farm
Marcus's wife, as she runs their household
The Senate, as it ruled over every Roman family
b.why: The paterfamilias held power over his household, and grown sons usually stayed under it for as long as he lived. Being an adult with a farm and a wife did not free Marcus while his father was alive.
b.clue: Does a son's age end his father's power in Roman law?

a.best: Plebeians, as wealth did not change his group

b.best: Titus, as the head of the family while he lives
